intro: Willem Mengelberg and the Concertgebouw Orchestra take Beethoven’s four-note opening from fierce octaves to the soft exchanges of the development. This is the first of two disc sides: the movement continues after the needle reaches the end.

sections.label: A · Three Gs and a fermata
sections.mNote: The opening rhythm passes through the strings

sections.label: B · Horn call and violin song
sections.mNote: E♭ major; repeated notes continue beneath the melody

sections.label: C · Fragments of the opening rhythm
sections.mNote: Short phrases pass between strings and winds

sections.label: D · Single chords across the silence
sections.mNote: Winds and strings take turns before the rhythm returns

cues.title: Three Gs, then a hold
cues.text: Beethoven begins with a rest, three Gs and an E♭ held under a fermata. Three Fs fall to a longer D. Mengelberg has two written pauses to shape before the strings begin passing the rhythm between them.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, I, bars 1–21; Mutopia 941, based on the Breitkopf & Härtel parts. Opening repeated notes, fermatas and subsequent string imitations.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A horn call opens out
cues.text: The horns keep the three-short-note rhythm and widen its intervals: B♭–B♭–B♭, E♭, F, B♭. The violins answer with a sweet E♭-major song. Below it, the cellos continue the little repeated-note figure.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 59–70; Mutopia 941, horns, first violins and cellos. Passage at the recording’s existing second-section boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A Telefunken disc in 1941
cues.text: Telefunken issues this performance in 1941. The Concertgebouw Orchestra plays under Mengelberg; SK 2210 carries the first part of the opening movement. A listener at home needs the other side to finish it.
cues.evidence: Musical Heritage Organization’s catalogue for Telefunken SK 2210 identifies Mengelberg, the Concertgebouw Orchestra, recording date 1939–40, first release 1941 and first-movement Part 1: http://pool.musicalheritage.org/index.php/Telefunken-sk2210-022110.

cues.title: One chord at a time
cues.text: The development pares the four-note rhythm down to slow chords. Winds and strings reply across rests, with Beethoven asking for ever softer playing. The thin exchanges eventually break open as the short repeated notes return.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 196–247; Mutopia 941, alternating minim chords, diminuendo, sempre più piano and returning repeated-note fragments. Passage at the existing final-section boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
